gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI sells a 560 W alternator charger, Charger 1, for $219 that it says works with all BLUETTI stations, and that it is sold bundled with the Elite 200 V2 for $1,099. It feeds the Elite 200 V2's 12–60 V / 20 A / 1,000 W solar input, so about 1.6 hours of driving puts back one 700 Wh e-bike charge, against the 96 W a 12 V socket gives.
standout_why: I compared it against our own cited page (dealectric.com), PowerStationGearLab (cited) and PowerBencher. Our page covers only the 96 W 12 V socket on the Elite 200 V2 and calls it too slow for a weekend. PowerStationGearLab covers pure sine output, solar wattage and expansion (DELTA 3 Max not expandable), but not car or alternator charging. PowerBencher says car input is not mentioned for any unit and that it tested no e-bike charger. No result names an alternator charger, its maker price, or which station it pairs with. None quotes an e-bike maker's own conditions for charging from an inverter (pure sine, at least 250 W, nothing else plugged in, and a possible warranty loss).
decides: It backs the Elite 200 V2 as the pick. Its main weakness, a thin margin for two charges (1,910 Wh measured against roughly 1,750–1,900 Wh needed), can be fixed with a maker-sold $219 accessory that refills it on the drive at 560 W. That makes a second charge plus camp loads realistic without moving up to the 3 kWh Elite 300. It also gives the page a maker-level caveat: one e-bike maker (Biktrix) says a non-grid source may void the warranty. Shoppers should check their own bike maker's policy before relying on any station.

findings.label: Alternator charger output and stated compatibility
findings.value: Max 560 W; 'Works with all BLUETTI power stations and most brands on the market'; ships with a DC input cable and an MC4 output cable
findings.note: The product page has no per-model compatibility table and no stated exclusions. Elite 200 V2 and AC180 appear only as bundle offers.

findings.label: Bundle with Charger 1, BLUETTI US store
findings.note: Price from storecheck.py on the BLUETTI Shopify store. That matches the station alone ($899) plus Charger 1 ($219) minus $19.

findings.label: Price alone, BLUETTI US store
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Portable Power Station | 2,600W 2,080Wh

findings.label: Solar (PV) input, the port Charger 1's MC4 output plugs into
findings.note: From the page FAQ. 560 W ÷ 20 A = 28 V, so Charger 1 needs an output of at least 28 V to deliver its full 560 W within this input's current limit. The 60 V ceiling leaves room for higher settings.

findings.label: Time to refill one 700 Wh e-bike charge from the car
findings.value: About 1.6 h of driving with Charger 1, against about 9 h from the 12 V socket
findings.note: This is arithmetic, not a measurement. A 700 Wh charge at the 80% wall-to-bike efficiency both ChatGPT answers and our page assume needs about 875 Wh from the station. 875 ÷ 560 W = 1.56 h. 875 ÷ 96 W (12 V socket figure on our page) = 9.1 h. Charger 1's own DC-DC losses are not included.

findings.label: Bundle with Charger 2, BLUETTI US store
findings.value: $1,299.00; BLUETTI lists Charger 2 as '1,200W car + solar charging'
findings.note: Bundle price from storecheck.py (https://www.bluettipower.com/products/charger-2-elite-200-v2). The same page also lists an Elite 300 + Charger 2 bundle. No wattage into each station is stated.

findings.label: An e-bike maker's conditions for charging from an inverter (Biktrix)
findings.value: Pure sine wave inverter supplying 110/220 V AC at 250 W or more, with nothing else connected; Biktrix says using a power source other than the grid can void the battery or charger warranty
findings.source_title: Can I charge my E-bike battery using an inverter? (Biktrix help)
findings.note: This is Biktrix's policy only. Other bike makers' policies were not found. It also advises against charging from the car battery with the engine running.

findings.label: Expansion battery
findings.value: Not expandable (PowerStationGearLab: 'EcoFlow's expandable version is the DELTA 3 Max Plus')
findings.source_title: Best Power Station for E-Bike Charging (2026) | PowerStationGearLab
findings.note: A cited rival page already states this, so it is not new.

findings.label: Expansion battery
findings.value: 2 kWh to 6 kWh with up to 2 extra batteries (PowerBencher)
findings.source_title: Best Portable Power Stations for E-Bikes and Scooters (2026) | PowerBencher
